strengths: The core idea — treating the 10-component spacetime metric tensor as a Neural Tensor Field ('Einstein Fields') whose dynamics emerge as a byproduct — is a genuinely interesting and well-motivated synthesis of neural fields with general relativity, clearly articulated and positioned relative to both the NeF and numerical relativity literatures.

The evaluation is unusually thorough and physics-aware: beyond standard MAE/rel-L2 on metric components, the authors validate derived quantities (Christoffel symbols, Riemann/Ricci/Weyl tensors, Kretschmann invariant), reconstruct classic GR phenomena (perihelion precession, Kerr geodesics, ring singularity, GW ring deformation, Ψ4, radiated power), and quantify rollout error accumulation — a sensitive test of metric quality.

Systematic ablations (Sobolev order, optimizer SOAP vs Adam, SiLU vs SIREN/WIRE, learning-rate schedule, metric vs distortion representation, coordinate charts) plus an honest Limitations section and a released open-source JAX differential geometry library support reproducibility.
The Sobolev (Jacobian/Hessian) supervision analysis showing when higher-order derivative supervision helps (curvature quantities) vs. hurts (geodesic rollouts) is a useful empirical contribution.
The paper demonstrates order-of-magnitude accuracy gains over 4th/6th-order finite-difference stencils for derivative quantities, and compelling visual outputs (black-hole rendering).
weaknesses: The central motivating claim — compressing 'computationally intensive four-dimensional numerical relativity simulations' into neural weights — is never actually demonstrated. All experiments fit smooth analytical solutions (Schwarzschild, Kerr, plane GWs), and the litmus test on real NR data (binary black hole/neutron star mergers) is explicitly deferred to future work. Fitting closed-form smooth fields is a much easier task that does not validate the compression or feasibility claims for genuine NR outputs.

The compression comparison is unfair in the demonstrated setting: analytic metrics are already maximally compact (given by formulas, or by spectral/spline representations far more accurate than 1e-8), and the Schwarzschild/Kerr cases are static (t=0 slice, effectively 3D). The claimed 1000–4000x compression relative to an explicit grid does not establish practical value.

Accuracy is a real limitation: best MAE ~1e-8, with the paper itself conceding that FD methods are only outperformed in FLOAT32, that spectral methods (the actual state of the art, which they acknowledge are 1000–5000x more efficient) are not compared against, and that geodesic rollout errors grow to δr ~ 0.1 (Schwarzschild) and behave erratically for Kerr — well below the precision NR demands.

Methodological novelty is limited: the technique is essentially an MLP fit with Sobolev derivative supervision plus AD — all established components. The contribution is primarily the application domain and the accompanying library, with substantial tutorial-style GR background (25+ pages of appendices) padding the paper relative to its novel technical content.

The coordinate-dependence of NeFs (errors varying by up to three orders of magnitude across charts, Table 9) is identified but unresolved, undermining the 'physics, not coordinates' desideratum the authors set out for themselves.

Numerous presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract and conclusion is empty/broken, typos ('Boyer-Lidquist', 'Zackiger orbits', 'tenors', 'Perihilion'), a leftover template artifact in Figure 2's caption ('/JBnot defined'), and a duplicated weak-grounding of GW usage claims — suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

No comparison against adaptive mesh refinement or Galerkin baselines for the derivative-reconstruction task, and the practical use cases (who needs a lossy, 1e-8-accurate continuous encoding of an already-analytic metric?) are not compellingly argued for the demonstrated setting.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and relatively unexplored intersection of neural fields and computational general relativity, and the framing of the metric tensor as a 'Neural Tensor Field' whose derivatives encode physics is a natural and appealing idea.

The experimental pipeline is physically grounded: evaluation goes beyond standard ML metrics to derived physical quantities (Christoffel symbols, Riemann/Ricci tensors, Kretschmann invariant, Weyl scalar Ψ4, geodesic rollouts, GW mode amplitudes), which is the right way to assess fidelity of a spacetime representation.

Comprehensive background and appendices, detailed hyperparameter reporting, ablation studies (optimizer, activation, Sobolev order, coordinate systems, distortion decomposition), and an open-source JAX library support reproducibility.

The Sobolev (Jacobian/Hessian) supervision study is reasonably thorough, including the useful negative finding that Hessian supervision can hurt geodesic rollouts while being necessary for curvature quantities.
weaknesses: The central claim — compressing 'computationally intensive four-dimensional numerical relativity simulations' — is not supported by the experiments. All use cases are exact analytic solutions (Schwarzschild, Kerr, linearized plane waves). Fitting closed-form expressions with MLPs does not demonstrate any value for actual NR simulation data, which the authors themselves defer to future work ('the litmus test'). The motivation built around petascale NR is therefore largely disconnected from what is shown.

The technical novelty is thin. The method reduces to a standard MLP coordinate network with Sobolev training (Czarnecki et al., 2017), off-the-shelf optimizers (SOAP), and AD-based construction of known differential-geometric quantities. The claim that 'dynamics emerge naturally as a byproduct' amounts to the fact that Christoffel symbols are functions of the metric and its first derivatives — a well-known mathematical identity, not a property of the neural representation.

Baseline comparisons are weak and somewhat misleading. The primary comparison is against naive finite-difference stencils applied to the ground-truth metric, while the paper's own Table 3 'GT (AD)' column shows the accuracy gains largely stem from AD, not from the neural representation. Spectral methods — which the paper itself notes are 1000–5000× more efficient than FD and effectively machine-precision accurate — are dismissed as future work, yet they already provide compact, highly accurate, differentiable representations that would directly compete with the claimed accuracy/storage advantages.

Quantitative geodesic results are weak relative to the claims: rollout deviations reach δr ≈ 0.1 (Schwarzschild) and δr ≈ 12 (Kerr) in units where the domain spans ~10, and orbits eventually diverge. Combined with the 1E−8 MAE ceiling in double precision, the practical precision advantage over double-precision classical methods is questionable.

Several technical and presentational issues undermine confidence: identical MAE values (6.24E-3 and 1.63E-6) reported for 'Christoffel Jacobian' and 'Metric Lie derivative' in Table 3; text referencing Figure 15 for a result shown in Figure 16; 'Zackiger' (presumably Zajicek) orbits; 'metric tenors'; an unfinished URL in the abstract; and a rendering artifact in Figure 2.

Significance for the NR/GR community is unclear. Compressing known analytic metrics with ~1M parameters offers limited utility; the interesting use cases (merger simulations, waveforms) are exactly those not demonstrated, and the authors acknowledge NeFs fail near singularities and high-curvature regions where NR matters most. The paper reads as a well-executed demonstration rather than a solution to a pressing problem.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framing: representing the spacetime metric as a neural tensor field ('Einstein Fields') is a genuinely new application of neural fields to general relativity, and the observation that dynamics (geodesics, curvature) emerge naturally via automatic differentiation from a metric representation is an attractive conceptual contribution.

Comprehensive physical validation beyond standard ML metrics: the paper reconstructs sensitive GR phenomena — perihelion precession, Kerr geodesics (retrograde/prograde/eccentric), Kretschmann invariant with ring singularity, GW ring deformation, Weyl scalar Ψ4, and radiated power — which serve as strong, physically meaningful checks of representation quality.

Thorough methodology study: systematic ablations over Sobolev supervision order (Jacobian/Hessian), optimizers (SOAP vs Adam), activation functions (SiLU vs SIREN/WIRE, with a thoughtful analysis of why oscillatory activations destabilize Sobolev training), learning-rate schedules, coordinate systems, and precision (FLOAT32 vs FLOAT64).

Honest and detailed limitations section: the authors clearly acknowledge the ~1E-8 MAE floor, error accumulation in long geodesic rollouts, failure near singularities, and coordinate-dependence of NeFs, and correctly note that the litmus test on real NR simulation data remains future work.

Significant community resource: an open-source JAX-based differential geometry library (tensor algebra, covariant/Lie derivatives, curvature quantities, analytical EFE solutions) with documented hardware, hyperparameters, and licenses, which should be useful beyond this paper.
Clear presentation pipeline: the Figures 1-3 DAGs connecting metric → Christoffel symbols → Riemann/Ricci/Weyl tensors via AD provide a clean conceptual and computational workflow.
weaknesses: Gap between central claim and evidence: the paper motivates Einstein Fields by the need to compress 'computationally intensive 4D numerical relativity simulations', but all experiments are on smooth analytical solutions (Schwarzschild, Kerr, linearized plane waves). Encoding known analytic functions is a much easier task than compressing genuine NR data with discontinuities, matter fields, or complex dynamics; the headline claim is therefore untested.

Weak compression baseline: the 1000-4000x compression factor is measured against an explicit grid representation, which the authors themselves admit is uncompetitive with spectral methods (they cite 1000-5000x spectral advantages over FD). Spectral representations would also be far more compact than grids and likely achieve better than 1E-8 accuracy, undermining the storage-efficiency claims.

Limited baseline diversity: comparisons are only against finite-difference stencils; no comparison with related learned-metric approaches (e.g., Li et al. 2023 solving Einstein equations with deep learning, Hirst et al. 2025) or with classical interpolation/spectral surrogate techniques on the same tasks.

Internal tension in the method: Hessian supervision improves tensor quantities (Tables 2-3) but degrades geodesic rollouts (Figure 12, Table 5), suggesting the training recipe is not uniformly beneficial and the choice is task-dependent without a principled resolution.

Accuracy ceiling is modest relative to the domain: best MAE of ~1E-8 with FLOAT64 evaluation still falls short of double-precision standards in numerical relativity, and errors accumulate erratically for Kerr orbits, limiting practical scientific use.

Presentation quality issues: several typos and broken references (e.g., '/JBnot defined' in Figure 2, 'metric tenors', inconsistent equation cross-references, 'Zackiger' orbits), and parts of the experiments are described only qualitatively (e.g., Figures 5, 7 orbit agreement) without quantitative error bounds in the main text.

Time-dependence is barely explored: Schwarzschild and Kerr experiments are trained at t=0 slices only; the sole temporally evolving case is an analytically trivial plane wave, so the ability to handle dynamic spacetimes — the core NR scenario — remains speculative.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated application domain: representing the metric tensor field of general relativity with neural tensor fields ('EinFields') is a sensible and, to my knowledge, new intersection of neural fields with numerical relativity, addressing a genuine storage/precision problem in NR workflows.

Careful GR-aware design choices: the distortion decomposition (Eq. 5), Sobolev training on metric Jacobian/Hessian to obtain accurate Christoffel symbols and curvature tensors, and coordinate-chart ablations show domain understanding beyond a naive INR application.

Thorough multi-level evaluation: compression and accuracy on analytic spacetimes (Schwarzschild, Kerr, linearized GWs), quantitative comparison against 4th/6th-order finite-difference stencils (Tables 1-2), physically meaningful downstream tasks (geodesics, perihelion precession, Kerr orbits, geodesic deviation, Weyl scalar Ψ4, Kretschmann scalar, black-hole rendering), and a realistic BSSN/FMR oscillating neutron-star simulation achieving ~2000× compression.

Honest and detailed limitations section (lossy compression, FLOAT64 requirement for rollouts, query latency, no AMR/spectral comparison), plus ablation studies (Table 4) on activations, optimizer (SOAP vs Adam), LR schedule, and derivative supervision, including a gradient-alignment analysis.

Reproducibility: open-source JAX library, hyperparameter tables (F.9), data generation configs, and hardware/software specification; the appendix supplies all mathematical background needed by both GR and ML audiences.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty from the ML side: the approach is essentially an MLP with Sobolev losses, SOAP optimizer, GradNorm, and Fourier features applied to a new domain; the paper itself notes these are known components (Sobolev training, PINN-adjacent techniques). The contribution is primarily an application/systems one, which may be considered thin by top-tier AI conference standards.

Missing comparison against classical/scientific compression baselines: the paper cites lossy HPC compression (SZ, JPEG2000, DWT, tensor decomposition, COIN-style neural compression) but evaluates only against raw grid storage and FD differentiation; without accuracy-vs-size curves for these baselines, the claimed 'up to 4000×' compression advantage is not fully substantiated.

Scope of dynamics is restricted: geodesic/analytic test beds are stationary or linearly time-dependent, and the sole NR case is a single oscillating star; the promised merger-type simulations (binary black hole / neutron star) are deferred to future work, limiting demonstrated significance to realistic NR pipelines. Additionally, rollouts require FLOAT64 and eventually diverge (Fig. 16), which weakens the claim of suitability for long-horizon dynamics.

Coordinate-system dependence of the learned representation is acknowledged but unresolved (Table 8 shows up to three orders of magnitude variation across charts; Cartesian KS is notably worse), and the paper offers no remedy, leaving a foundational question for a framework whose subject is a covariant theory.

Presentation quality issues reduce polish: 'CONLUSION', 'Higer-order', 'Tekoulsky', a leftover '[specify hardware]' placeholder in the Reproducibility Statement, duplicated 'Definition 2' labels, and a partially garbled sentence in Appendix E suggest insufficient proofreading. The ~45 pages of tutorial-style GR appendices also bury the experimental content.

Reported derivative accuracy gains (up to 10^5 over FD) are mostly on uniform-grid toy settings in FLOAT32; for the NR simulation case, the FD comparison uses a fourth-order stencil on stability grounds and Christoffel MAE of 8.61e-4 (Table 13) is considerably less impressive than the analytic-case results, so headline claims are stronger than the hardest-evidence results.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored intersection: applying neural-field representations to the metric tensor of general relativity, with a principled pipeline for deriving geometric quantities (Christoffel symbols, Riemann/Weyl tensors, curvature invariants) via automatic differentiation.

The evaluation is broad along multiple axes: compression ratios (~1000-4000x), derivative accuracy vs. higher-order finite differences, physical fidelity checks (geodesics, perihelion precession, gravitational-wave strain), and a realistic BSSN/Einstein Toolkit neutron-star simulation.

Thorough ablations (distortion parameterization, activation functions, optimizer, Sobolev levels, coordinate systems) and an unusually honest limitations section (lossy compression, FLOAT64 requirement for rollouts, prohibitive query latency, no AMR/spectral benchmarks).
An open-source JAX library, extensive appendices, and hyperparameter documentation support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core recipe is a standard MLP implicit neural representation with Sobolev (derivative) losses and a SOAP/GradNorm training stack - all well-established techniques. The contribution is primarily an application of existing machinery to a new data domain, and the 'Neural Tensor Fields' framing adds little technical substance beyond calling the output a tensor.

The headline claims rest mostly on analytic, smooth benchmarks (Schwarzschild, Kerr, linearized gravity waves) that are essentially ideal test cases for smooth function approximators; compression factors and derivative-accuracy gains are expected a priori in this regime and do not establish value on the hard problems (e.g., binary mergers with turbulence, sharp gradients, AMR) that motivate the paper's introduction.

Missing or weak baselines: no comparison against established scientific compression methods (SZ, ZFP, tensor decomposition/Tucker, wavelet INRs like the cited Masked Wavelet Representation) or against spectral/spline interpolation, which the paper itself notes can be 1000-5000x faster than FD. The FD stencil is arguably a strawman baseline for differentiation accuracy.

The realistic NR demonstration is limited to a single oscillating TOV snapshot; it is unclear the method handles the time-evolving, 4D, matter-coupled simulations that constitute actual NR practice, and this limitation is deferred to future work.

Several practical concerns undermine the utility claims: reported query times (ms per 1e5 batch), the need for FLOAT64 in geodesic rollouts with accumulating errors (Fig. 16), and the unexplained three-order-of-magnitude sensitivity to coordinate chart (Table 8), which sits uneasily with claims of mesh/coordinate independence.

Presentation and rigor issues: typos ('Higer-order', 'CONLUSION', 'tekoulsky', 'convential'), a placeholder left in the reproducibility statement ('[specify hardware]'), and claims of 'resolutions of 1e-7 - 1e-9' that are inconsistent with the caveat that these errors 'lack immediate physical meaning' and that sub-1e-9 accuracy is unattainable.

No theoretical analysis of when or why the representation should preserve the differential-geometric structure (e.g., Bianchi identity residuals are only reported pointwise for one metric), and no error propagation analysis from metric error to curvature quantities.

strengths: Genuine novelty in the problem setting: to my knowledge this is the first systematic treatment of implicit neural representations of 4D spacetime metrics, framing the work as 'Neural Tensor Fields' where geometry, dynamics (geodesics), and curvature are derived as byproducts via automatic differentiation. This opens a concrete new direction at the intersection of neural fields and numerical relativity.

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple axes: compression ratios (1000–4000x), derivative accuracy versus sixth-order FD stencils (1–5 orders of magnitude), physical validation via canonical GR tests (Schwarzschild/Kerr geodesics, gravitational wave strain, Weyl scalars, Kretschmann invariants), ablations (metric distortion, activation functions, optimizers, Sobolev levels), sensitivity to coordinate charts (Table 8), and a realistic BSSN/FMR neutron-star simulation with proper octree-style (SMR) analysis (Table 14).

Honest and unusually detailed limitations section: acknowledges lossy compression, FLOAT64 requirement for geodesic rollouts, long-time divergence of trajectories, prohibitive query latency, and the omission of AMR/spectral baselines. The gradient-alignment analysis (Appendix F.5) provides useful insight into Sobolev training dynamics.

Good engineering contribution: an open-source JAX library, complete training algorithm, hyperparameter tables, and detailed pedagogical background making the paper accessible to both ML and GR audiences.

Physically meaningful evaluation design: the paper is careful to validate on coordinate-independent observables (Ricci scalar, Kretschmann invariant, geodesic deviation) rather than component-level errors alone, and to distinguish true from coordinate singularities.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core machinery is a straightforward composition of existing components (SIREN/WIRE-style INRs, Sobolev derivative losses, SOAP optimizer, GradNorm weighting). The primary contribution is application and integration rather than new learning techniques, which bounds the paper's impact on the broader AI community.

Weak baselines on the central compression claim: the 4000x compression factor is measured only against uncompressed explicit grids. There is no comparison against established lossy compression codecs (SZ, ZFP, tensor decompositions — the latter are cited but not compared), nor against faster INR variants (e.g., hash-grid/multiresolution encodings), which would likely change the accuracy–storage–query-time tradeoff analysis substantially.

Practical utility concerns are understated: reported query latency (a few ms per 1e5 queries) and 100–2000s per-field training are workable for static spacetimes, but the workflow does not yet demonstrate compression of a genuinely time-evolving 4D NR simulation end-to-end (the neutron-star case trains on coalesced time-slice grids); binary mergers, the real storage bottleneck motivating the paper, are deferred to future work.

Precision gap with the target domain: NR workflows require accuracies well beyond 1e-7 relative error, and the authors themselves show geodesic rollouts diverge and curvature quantities are unstable at single precision. This weakens the claim of fitness for realistic NR pipelines beyond compression/visualization use cases.

Presentation issues that should not appear at this quality level: placeholder text in the reproducibility statement ('[specify hardware, e.g., ...]'), and multiple typos ('Higer-order', 'CONLUSION', 'Perihilion', 'Minkowksi', 'Tekoulsky'), suggesting the manuscript was not fully polished before submission.

Some claims are phrased too strongly relative to evidence (e.g., 'first implicit neural framework... suitable for downstream tasks') given that the demonstrated downstream tasks are analytic testbeds and one static-refinement simulation, and the coordinate-choice sensitivity (up to three orders of magnitude, Table 8) is noted but unresolved.
